newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian '96 cocoa imports flat, may pick up in '97.
newsitem.headline: Russian '96 cocoa imports flat, may pick up in '97.

text.p: Russia's 1996 cocoa imports are likely to be around 1995 levels, but could increase next year as domestic consumers desert Western sweets in favour of Russian brands, trade and industry officials said on Thursday.
"We forecast total cocoa bean imports in 1996 at some 75,000-80,000 tonnes, or roughly the same amount as in 1995," said a Russian trader who declined to be named.
Official statistics from the State Customs Committee show that Russia imported 51,400 tonnes of cocoa beans in 1995, but the numbers do not account for undeclared deliveries.
In the Soviet era, Russia consumed over 100,000 tonnes of cocoa beans a year.
While traders say a return to such volumes is some way off, they forecast imports could begin recovering next year, as domestic confectionery manufacturers begin to boost output.

"This year, we are likely to buy the same amount of cocoa beans as last year, but we do not exclude that 1997 purchases could be larger," said a senior Babayevsky confectionery factory official, who declined to provide figures.
An official from the State Statistics Committee said Russia imported 32,200 tonnes of cocoa beans in the first seven months of this year, a five percent rise from year-ago levels.

"Imports of cocoa beans could rise next year, whereas purchases of Western-made output containing cocoa could fall," one Moscow-based trader said. He said most of the total was for beans, with little buying of cocoa butter or liquor.

The official from Babayevsky, a leading sweets maker in Moscow, said overall domestic chocolate consumption would be stable this year. But he expected demand for Russian products to rise next year by 20 to 30 percent.
"Domestic consumers have tasted all those Mars and Snickers bars just to find out that our chocolate is better," he said.
Western chocolate makers counter that their products are unlikely to lose market share.
"Our business is going well in Russia," said a Nestle's source in Moscow who declined to be named.

Alexander Pavlov, head of the Food Industry Department at the Agriculture Ministry, said he expected output of domestic chocolates to rise by eight percent in 1997 due to confectionery plants' remodernisation plans and changing consumption trends.
"Our chocolate wasn't considered bad in the past, before this massive influx of foreign sweets," Pavlov said.
"But Russia does not grow cocoa beans, and if there are plans to produce more Russian chocolate, then there must be higher cocoa imports."

Imports of cocoa beans and derivatives by the Soviet Union, including Russia, which accounted for 75 percent of the country's buying, varied from 150,000 to 180,000 tonnes a year before the country collapsed in 1991, traders say.
The Nestle's source said one strong point at domestic sweets' makers was packaging chocolates in bright gift boxes for holidays.
"In fact, now there are big purchases of these in view of the forthcoming Christmas and New Year. But our chocolate snacks are for everyday consumption." --Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
